title: Session cookie issued without Secure flag on HTTPS-terminated (proxy) requests
description: The `PHPSESSID` session cookie is only marked `Secure` when the PHP variable `$_SERVER['HTTPS']` is literally set. When TLS is terminated by a reverse proxy that signals HTTPS through `X-Forwarded-Proto` (or `SERVER_PORT=443`) instead of setting `HTTPS`, the application still treats the connection as HTTPS for other features (HSTS is emitted) but issues the session cookie **without** the `Secure` attribute. The cookie can therefore be transmitted over cleartext HTTP, exposing the session to interception.
impact: If the deployment sits behind a TLS-terminating proxy (the documented canonical deployment is `https://dimspersonal.my.id`), the session cookie is not restricted to HTTPS. An attacker positioned to observe or force a single cleartext HTTP request (e.g., a downgrade link, an `http://` subresource/redirect, or a network adversary) can capture a valid `PHPSESSID` and hijack the authenticated session of any role, including `admin`. This undermines the confidentiality of all authenticated functionality (violation records, reports, user actions, admin news/tatib CRUD).
technical_analysis:
Session cookie parameters are configured in a single place:

```php title=helpers/token_helper.php startLineNumber=13 endLineNumber=17
session_set_cookie_params([
    'secure' => (!empty($_SERVER['HTTPS']) && $_SERVER['HTTPS'] !== 'off'),
    'httponly' => true,
    'samesite' => 'Lax',
]);
```

The `secure` value depends solely on `$_SERVER['HTTPS']`. It does **not** consider `X-Forwarded-Proto` or `SERVER_PORT`, unlike the rest of the application. `helpers/seo_helper.php` (lines 219-222 and 146-151) determines HTTPS from `$_SERVER['HTTPS']` **or** `SERVER_PORT === '443'` **or** `HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO === 'https'`, and emits `Strict-Transport-Security` on that basis (lines 227-229).

The result is an internal inconsistency: on a request the application itself classifies as HTTPS (HSTS emitted), the session cookie is not marked `Secure`. This was confirmed against the running instance by sending `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` with a non-local `Host`: the response carried the HSTS header but the `Set-Cookie` line lacked `Secure`.
poc_description:
1. Send a request that the application classifies as HTTPS via the forwarded-proto signal, using a non-local `Host` so the HSTS branch is taken.
2. Observe the response headers.
3. Note that `Strict-Transport-Security` is present (application believes the request is HTTPS) while the `Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=...` line omits the `Secure` attribute.
4. Repeating without the header (or with `Host` local) produces the same cookie flags, confirming `secure` is never set when `$_SERVER['HTTPS']` is absent.
poc_script_code:
```bash
# Response is treated as HTTPS (HSTS emitted) yet the session cookie lacks Secure
curl -s -i -H "X-Forwarded-Proto: https" -H "Host: dimspersonal.my.id" \
  http://172.17.112.1:8001/login -D - -o /dev/null | grep -iE "set-cookie|strict-transport"
```

Observed:

```http
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=hh5q0hgt2qii0p2q2dd06juaqh; path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload
```
remediation_steps: Determine the request scheme using the same logic already used elsewhere in the application (a single shared helper). Mark the session cookie `Secure` whenever the request is HTTPS by any of: `$_SERVER['HTTPS']` set, `SERVER_PORT` equal to `443`, or `X-Forwarded-Proto: https`. Only trust forwarded headers from known proxy addresses. As defence in depth, enable `session.cookie_secure` and consider HSTS `preload` plus an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect so no cleartext request can carry the cookie.
evidence:
Request (application treats as HTTPS):

```http
GET /login HTTP/1.1
Host: dimspersonal.my.id
X-Forwarded-Proto: https
```

Response (note HSTS present, cookie lacks `Secure`):

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=hh5q0hgt2qii0p2q2dd06juaqh; path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload
```

Baseline plain HTTP:

```http
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=1pbhqcjlkd5f40aj7uatn49ma8; path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
```
assumptions: Assumes the production deployment terminates TLS at a reverse proxy that conveys the scheme via `X-Forwarded-Proto`/`SERVER_PORT` rather than setting `$_SERVER['HTTPS']`, which is consistent with the application's canonical URL (`https://dimspersonal.my.id`) and its own proxy-aware HTTPS detection elsewhere. On the provided lab target (plain HTTP) the same code path yields no `Secure` by design.

title: No absolute session lifetime and no invalidation of concurrent sessions
description: The application enforces only a 30-minute **idle** timeout that is reset on every request; there is no absolute session lifetime. In addition, an account may hold an unlimited number of simultaneous sessions, and a new login does not invalidate existing sessions. A captured session cookie therefore remains usable indefinitely as long as it is used periodically, and logging in again does not revoke a hijacked session.
impact: A stolen session cookie is valid for the entire browsing lifetime of the victim rather than being bounded by an absolute cap, and re-authentication does not evict the attacker. Combined with the missing `Secure` attribute, a captured `PHPSESSID` provides durable, unaudited access as the victim (including `admin`), extending the window for data theft and fraudulent state changes.
poc_description:
1. Authenticate the same account twice from two independent cookie jars.
2. Confirm both session identifiers remain simultaneously valid against a protected page (`/pelanggaran` or `/pelanggaran/dosen`) returning HTTP 200.
3. Continue issuing requests on the older session; observe it is never invalidated by the newer login.
4. (Lifetime) Programmatically, only `__last_activity` is checked; there is no creation timestamp or absolute cap, so periodic requests keep the session alive without limit.
poc_script_code:
```bash
login() { # user pass type jar
  jar=$4; rm -f $jar
  tok=$(curl -s -c $jar http://172.17.112.1:8001/login \
        | grep -o 'name="csrf_token" value="[0-9a-f]*"' | grep -o '[0-9a-f]\{64\}' | head -1)
  curl -s -o /dev/null -b $jar -c $jar -X POST http://172.17.112.1:8001/action/login \
       --data-urlencode "csrf_token=$tok" --data-urlencode "user_type=$3" \
       --data-urlencode "username=$1" --data-urlencode "password=$2"
}

login 1234567890 password123 dosen cA.txt
login 1234567890 password123 dosen cB.txt   # second session, same account

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "A /pelanggaran/dosen -> %{http_code}\n" -b cA.txt http://172.17.112.1:8001/pelanggaran/dosen
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "B /pelanggaran/dosen -> %{http_code}\n" -b cB.txt http://172.17.112.1:8001/pelanggaran/dosen
# both return 200 => concurrent sessions coexist, neither revoked
```
remediation_steps: Store a session creation timestamp (e.g., `__created_at`) at login and reject the session after an absolute lifetime (for example 8-12 hours) regardless of activity, forcing re-authentication. Track the server-side session inventory per user and, on each successful login (and on password change), invalidate all other sessions for that account. Optionally cap concurrent sessions and require re-authentication for logout. Enable server-side session garbage collection with a matching `gc_maxlifetime`.
evidence:
Two live sessions for the same `dosen` account (both HTTP 200 on protected page):

```text
SID A=iqpeoc735qma9vhsnij5drbit7  SID B=qah2ohf6fvcctj0mf1p07r8js5
A -> 200
B -> 200
```

Two live sessions for the same `mahasiswa` account:

```text
SID1(original)=408jn9og18nlgvd8clfu4vvoed  SID2(new)=9m3rov404rm2ih910h6g4i2pkf
SID1 /pelanggaran -> 200
SID2 /pelanggaran -> 200
```

The idle timer is refreshed on every request, so continuous activity keeps the session alive with no upper bound.

```php title=helpers/token_helper.php startLineNumber=107 endLineNumber=119
$lastActivity = isset($_SESSION['__last_activity']) ? (int) $_SESSION['__last_activity'] : 0;
if ($lastActivity > 0 && ($now - $lastActivity) > $idleTtl) {
    // ...expire...
}
$_SESSION['__last_activity'] = $now; // refreshed on every request
```
assumptions: Assumes an attacker who has captured a session cookie (e.g., via the missing-Secure issue, a shared/untrusted device, or network interception). The findings are configuration/lifecycle weaknesses that do not by themselves grant access without a stolen session or a compromised browser. The concurrency observation applies to any authenticated account, including `admin`.
